title: Cheerful in pain
hookLine: from Apollonius: steadiness, and staying the same in sharp pain and long illness (Meditations 1.8)

lines: YOU CAN'T LEARN IT FROM A BOOK.
A PHILOSOPHER FROM ACROSS THE SEA.
cards: Some things you can't learn from a book. You learn them by watching someone hurt.
The next name on Marcus's list of debts is a philosopher from across the sea, and what Marcus took from him was a way of being in sharp pain, in grief and in long illness. Today: cheerful in pain.

teach.b: First, Apollonius. A Stoic philosopher, said to come from Chalcedon, on the far side of the Bosporus, he was brought to Rome to teach the young Marcus.

A later Roman biography says he insisted the pupil come to him, not the other way round, and that the emperor Antoninus joked it was easier for Apollonius to travel all the way to Rome than across the city from his house to the palace.
True or not, it fits a man who wouldn't bend his dignity. Second, the line.

teach.h: THE SAME IN PAIN, GRIEF, LONG ILLNESS.
teach.b: From Apollonius, Marcus says in Long's translation, he learned "to be always the same, in sharp pains, on the occasion of the loss of a child, and in long illness."
Three kinds of suffering: sudden pain, grief, and the long grinding kind. The same person through all three. Third, read it knowing Marcus.
He was often unwell; the historian Cassius Dio says his health was poor, especially his chest and stomach. And he and his wife Faustina buried children of their own.
When he wrote the loss of a child, he wasn't imagining it. Fourth, what else Apollonius showed.

teach.h: FIRM, GENTLE, AND GOOD AT RECEIVING.
teach.b: He was firm, and yet gentle. He thought his skill as a teacher was the least of his gifts.
And Marcus learned from him how to accept favors from friends without groveling or brushing them off, an echo of Seneca's lesson on receiving well, from a different teacher.
Cheerful here doesn't mean smiling through pain. It means pain doesn't get to change who you are.

how: People who draw on this passage often practice staying even-tempered with others while they are ill or grieving, without pretending the pain isn't there.

o: the teacher who showed Marcus how to stay the same in pain
the doctor who treated Marcus's chest and stomach pains
a priest of Apollo who healed the sick at a Greek temple

games.q: cheerful in pain — tap the pairs.

s: 'cheerful in pain' means smiling and pretending nothing hurts
the line is about staying the same person, not hiding the pain.
Marcus mentions the loss of a child in this entry
and he and Faustina buried children of their own.
Apollonius taught that his skill as a teacher was his greatest gift
Marcus says Apollonius counted it the least of his merits.

games.q: you're Apollonius, the well-known teacher, and the emperor's heir needs lessons. where do they happen?
o: you go to the palace, as asked.
you send a student in your place.
games.why: a later biography says Apollonius insisted the pupil come to him. it's a story, not certain, but it fits his firmness.

practice: Notice one small discomfort in your body right now, a tight shoulder, an ache, a too-hard chair, and stay beside it without fighting or fixing it: the same breath, the same face, the same kindness toward yourself.
If you live with real pain, be gentle; this isn't a test.

wordCard.voice: Apollonius. The Stoic teacher from whom Marcus learned to stay the same person in sharp pain, in grief, and in long illness. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: 'the same'. The heart of what Marcus learned from Apollonius.

carryVoice: Your line: the same in pain. Firm, and yet gentle, like the teacher who showed it. Day five hundred twenty-five, the end of a week.
